newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa discusses cooperation with Rwanda.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa discusses cooperation with Rwanda.

text.p: South Africa said on Wednesday it was discussing economic and military cooperation with the Rwandan government to help rebuild the central African country crippled by ethnic conflict.

South African Deputy President Thabo Mbeki held talks with visiting Rwandan Vice President Major General Paul Kagame in Pretoria on Wednesday and said they would sign a memorandum of understanding on cooperation before the end of the week.

Mbeki said Rwanda faced many challenges after a 1994 genocide of minority Tutsis by Hutu hardliners and the resettlement of millions of refugees who fled to the former Zaire, and who were now returning home.

"The South African government recognises the special and urgent situation affecting Rwanda because of the genocide and the resettlement of people. We believe this requires exceptional attention," Mbeki told reporters.

He said the South African government would provide technical expertise to Rwanda in the financial and commodities sectors, and with the help of the private sector would look at rebuilding Rwanda's infrastructure and energy sector.
South Africa could also help to develop Rwandan's large methane gas deposits through its chemical's firm Sasol Ltd and its state-owned oil from gas producer Mossgas, Mbeki said.
Cooperation in water management, health, agriculture and education was also being discussed.

South African government officials have also begun advising the new government of Laurent Kabila's Democratic Republic of the Congo, formerly Zaire, on reconstruction of that country's fiscal infrastructure.

Mbeki has been a leading mediator in conflicts in the Great Lakes region and was the first high-ranking African leader to visit Kabila after he proclaimed himself president of the former Zaire, Africa's third-largest country.

He said South Africa was concerned about Rwanda's security situation with continuing attacks in the country by alleged Hutu militiamen who played a leading role in the 1994 genocide and who are now among refugees returning to their homeland.

"We are concerned that the government of Rwanda should have the capacity to protect itself. We really believe that the security needs of Rwanda needs to be addressed and we will be discussing military cooperation," Mbeki said, but did not elaborate.
Kagame, who is also Rwanda's defence minister, said he welcomed South Africa's support.
"Our ambition in Rwanda is to survive," he told reporters, referring to continued threats by Hutu militia.
Kagame said Rwanda had supported Kabila's ouster of former Zairean President Mobutu Sese Seko, but declined to elaborate.

He did not comment on accusations that Tutsi officers of the Rwandanese army had ordered massacres of Rwandan Hutu refugees inside the Congo during the rebel campaign, saying only that he would welcome an unbiased inquiry into the charges.

"We welcome an impartial investigation into what happened," he said, adding that the composition of the investigation team should be left to the Congo. The United Nations has said it will send a new delegation to the region to probe the allegations.
